item.title: Entrepreneurial Ecosystems in Emerging Economies
item.content:encoded:
Ioana Stefan, Mälardalen University

Ikenna Uzuegbunam, Howard University

Brett Anitra Gilbert, American University

Wim Vanhaverbeke, Antwerp University

Kadigia Faccin, Fundação Dom Cabral

Yanbo Wang, University of Hong Kong

Entrepreneurial ecosystems are essential for economic growth, yet research has predominantly focused on developed economies and urban contexts. This special issue seeks to address the underrepresentation of emerging economy research by examining entrepreneurial ecosystems across Africa, Asia, South America, and other developing regions. The issue recognizes that emerging economies face distinct challenges including weak institutions, high uncertainty, limited market sizes, and infrastructure gaps that fundamentally shape how ecosystems develop and function differently than in advanced economies.

The special issue invites research that balances Global North and Global South perspectives, examines ecosystem temporality and evolution, applies systems thinking to understand broader societal impacts, considers multi-level interactions from individual to macro levels, and explores how digitalization uniquely affects emerging economy contexts. Contributors are encouraged to investigate governmental initiatives like Startup Chile and Startup India and to address how entrepreneurial ecosystems can support sustainable development and circular economy practices in developing regions.

Appel publié par Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal. Voir l'appel sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How entrepreneurial ecosystems emerge, develop and evolve over time in emerging economies compared to advanced economies
  • The role of local and national culture in shaping entrepreneurial ecosystems across different contexts
  • How entrepreneurial ecosystems support refugees, diasporan and returnee entrepreneurs
  • The role of local and international venture funding instruments in emerging economies' entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Lifecycles and temporal structures of entrepreneurial ecosystems in emerging economies
  • Historical perspectives on entrepreneurial ecosystems and the impact of historical events on their emergence
  • Systems approaches to entrepreneurial ecosystems and their co-evolution with other structures
  • How entrepreneurial ecosystems impact society beyond economic benefits
  • Building blocks of sustainable and resilient entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Policy effectiveness in supporting entrepreneurial ecosystems in emerging economies
  • Multi-level analysis of interactions between individual, organizational and ecosystem levels
  • Institutional distrust, corruption and their influence on ecosystem orchestration
  • How digitalization and digital technologies shape emergent forms of ecosystems in emerging economies
  • Digital technologies and infrastructures transforming the geography of entrepreneurship in emerging economies

Timeline

  • April 30, 2027: Submission deadline

Associate editors

  • David Sirmon, University of Washington

item.title: International Entrepreneurship In An Age Of Persistent Disruption
item.content:encoded:
Olga Petričević, University of Calgary

Christos N. Pitelis, National and Kapodistrian University of Athens

Stratos Ramoglou, University of Bristol

Catherine L. Wang, Brunel University of London

Shaker A. Zahra, University of Minnesota

This special issue examines how entrepreneurial firms navigate systematic disruption in international markets. Rather than treating disruption as temporary shocks, the issue positions continuous, cascading disruptions—including geopolitical tensions, technological change, regulatory fragmentation, and supply chain disruption—as the permanent operating environment for internationally active ventures. The challenge is to understand how these firms adapt their internationalization strategies, timing, and value creation approaches when traditional market entry logic and past experience no longer provide guidance.

Appel publié par Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How do geopolitical bifurcation and regulatory fragmentation reshape opportunity structures for entrepreneurial internationalization?
  • How do entrepreneurial firms experiment with and strategically recalibrate the timing of internationalization in response to unfolding disruptions? Do timing choices and decision rules differ between gradual and sudden disruptions?
  • What are emerging forms of temporary, relational, or ecosystem-based advantage in turbulent environments for entrepreneurial firms that internationalize?
  • How do the new realities of the global marketplace impact entrepreneurial ventures' foreign market entry modes, and how does this reshape competitive strategies and modes of competition?
  • How do internationally oriented entrepreneurial ventures develop and deploy forms of strategic dexterity to orchestrate heterogeneous resources, partners, and knowledge flows across fragmented and institutionally diverse global ecosystems?
  • How do digital infrastructures and interorganizational alliances reconfigure the sensing, seizing, and transforming capabilities and their microfoundations in IE, and how do these enablers shape the balance between agility and strategic control across borders?
  • How do internationally active entrepreneurial ventures develop and deploy non-market and political capabilities to orchestrate resilience, legitimacy, and innovation within a polycentric, digitally mediated, and institutionally fragmented global order, and what strategic learning mechanisms enable effective navigation across world regions?
  • To what extent do dynamic capabilities retain relevance for entrepreneurial internationalization in contexts of heightened technological turbulence, geopolitical volatility, and ecosystemic interdependence?
  • How do internationally active entrepreneurial firms strategically orchestrate cross-border knowledge creation, transfer, and protection in the face of increasingly restrictive IP regimes, data localization policies, and digital sovereignty constraints?
  • How does the evolving mobility of talent, ideas, and digital capital under disruption reconfigure the spatial and cognitive geographies of international entrepreneurial ecosystems and innovation hotspots, and with what implications for business model innovation and evolution?
  • What governance mechanisms enable IE firms to build trust, coordinate value creation, and protect IP across fragmented institutional contexts?
  • How is the strategic logic of international location and embeddedness evolving for entrepreneurial firms amid digital virtualization, geopolitical realignment, and shifting global value networks?

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline

Associate editors

  • Yong Li, University of Nevada, Las Vegas

item.title: Mobilizing, Organizing, and Exploiting Entrepreneurial Judgment Within Ecosystems
item.content:encoded:
David B. Audretsch, Indiana University Bloomington

Maksim Belitski, University of Reading

Rosa Caiazza, Parthenope University of Naples

Nicolai J. Foss, Copenhagen Business School

Donald Siegel, Arizona State University

This special issue examines how entrepreneurial judgment operates within ecosystems involving multiple stakeholders rather than individual entrepreneurs or single firms. While entrepreneurial judgment under uncertainty has traditionally been studied at the individual or firm level, modern entrepreneurship increasingly unfolds through collaborations, alliances, and digital ecosystems where judgment must be communicated, coordinated, and governed among various actors. The issue seeks to advance understanding of ecosystem governance mechanisms and how judgment is mobilized and exploited to support cooperation, competition, and innovation.

Appel publié par Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Communicating tacit judgment in ecosystems
  • Governance and orchestration mechanisms in entrepreneurial ecosystems
  • Partial communicability and protection of entrepreneurial knowledge
  • Distributed judgment and performance across multiple stakeholders
  • Ecosystem dynamics, maturity and role structure
  • AI and decision-support tools in entrepreneurial ecosystems

Timeline

  • March 1, 2027: Deadline for full paper submissions

Associate editors

  • Peter Klein, Baylor University

item.title: Resource Orchestration for Competitive Advantage In Family Firms: Leveraging Financial And Non-Financial Resources
item.content:encoded:
R. Duane Ireland, Texas A&M University

Francesco Chirico, Macquarie University

Melissa E. Graebner, University of Illinois

Luis R. Gómez-Mejía, Arizona State University

Daniel Pittino, Jonkoping University

Family firms differ from non-family firms in their resource portfolios and resource orchestration processes, particularly regarding how they integrate financial and non-financial resources. Resource orchestration comprises three interconnected processes—structuring, bundling, and leveraging—that enable firms to build and deploy capabilities for competitive advantage. Family firms face unique challenges because family members often incorporate both financial and non-financial utilities into strategic decisions, with socioemotional wealth playing a central role in preserving family control, emotional attachment, social ties, and intergenerational continuity.

Appel publié par Strategic Entrepreneurship Journal. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

  • Role of legacy in family firms' engagement with strategic entrepreneurship
  • Stakeholder enrollment's role in family firms' resource acquisition for strategic entrepreneurship
  • Implications of succession and ownership transfers on family firms' strategic entrepreneurship
  • Structures supporting founders' and founding teams' decisions to use strategic entrepreneurship for family-based start-ups
  • Optimal combinations of identity, justice, and nepotism dimensions for maximizing resource orchestration and strategic entrepreneurship value
  • How different governance structures shape family firms' resource structuring, bundling, and leveraging decisions
  • Conditions under which dual focus on financial and non-financial objectives results in path dependency versus sustainable innovation
